findings.fix: Lengthen two distractors per question to the key's length with an equally specific, wrong reason, or trim the keys.

findings.quote: Shuffling the days before you split is the fairest way to test a forecast, because it removes the calendar's influence.
findings.problem: False, and the opposite of what the lesson teaches. Shuffled hold-outs put every tested day between days the model trained on, so a flexible model is flattered; they do not remove the calendar's influence, they leak it. It contradicts seg1, seg2, the predict reveal, quiz q1, both drills and the first take-away of the same lesson.
findings.evidence: forecast.shuffled_folds_vs_backtest.gradient_boosting_on_calendar: mape_shuffled_folds 0.0318 vs mape_backtest 0.0541. Principle: a forecast is evaluated out of time, from a past origin forward.
findings.fix: Delete the sentence. The segment should end on 'A best case, not a promise.'

findings.where: quiz 6-2-q2, with seg5 narration and ask_assistant
findings.quote: Finance asks for next month's spend as 'just one number'. Your backtests show that actual spend fell within roughly 4 percent of the daily forecast on four days out of five.
findings.problem: The only range the lesson builds is for one day's value (percentiles of daily percentage errors), yet the question, the opening ask and the transfer items hand it over with a monthly figure. A range for a total has to come from backtest errors of totals: daily misses partly cancel in a sum (or, after a level shift, do not), so the daily band is the wrong width for the month. Here it is about four times too wide, and nothing in the lesson says the band is per day only.
findings.evidence: forecast.interval.how: 10th and 90th percentiles of the regression's daily percentage errors, -0.0449 to +0.0381. forecast.backtest.methods.trend_plus_seasonality_regression.error_of_28_day_total_typical = 0.0097.
findings.fix: Add to seg5: 'That band is for a single day. For the month's total, build the range the same way from the backtests' 28-day totals; here the total typically misses by about 1 percent.' In q2 either ask about daily spend or quote a band measured on totals; add the totals band to ask_assistant.

findings.quote: Nobody is thrown away, and nobody is assumed to have stayed or gone.
findings.problem: The curve does rest on an assumption that is never stated: advertisers who drop out of view face the same week-by-week risk as those still watched. With join dates spread over two years, the far end of the curve is estimated from the oldest cohorts only; if newer advertisers churn differently (a new acquisition channel, a product change) the median is wrong for today's customers. The lesson says the tail 'rests on the fewest people' but not that it rests on the earliest joiners.
findings.evidence: Principle: Kaplan-Meier requires censoring to be unrelated to churn risk (no cohort drift). time_to_event.setup: 'joined at different times over the last two years'.
findings.fix: Add one sentence: 'This assumes recent joiners behave like earlier ones at the same tenure; check it by drawing the curve separately by join period.' Add the by-join-period curve to the audit checklist.

findings.where: other_ways item 2 ('Embeddings with a simple trained model'), and seg7 narration
findings.quote: When you have labelled examples and a high volume of text, or the text must not leave the building.
findings.problem: In this course the embeddings come from a hosted embedding model, so the ticket text leaves the building exactly as it does for the language models; lesson 7-2 says so in its limits and its audit list. Seg7 also presents 'the text leaves the building' as a cost of the language-model rungs alone. A learner following this would route confidential text through an embedding service believing it stays in-house.
findings.evidence: tickets.embedding_model = "gemini-embedding-2", a vendor model from the same family as the two classifiers (tickets.models). Lesson 7-2 seg7: 'embedding a ticket means sending its text to a model. Know where it goes.'; 7-2 other_ways gives word counts, not embeddings, as the route when 'the text must stay in-house'.
findings.fix: other_ways: '...or, with an embedding model you run in-house, when the text must not leave the building.' Seg7: say that of the five rungs only keyword rules and the bag-of-words model keep the text in-house by default.

findings.quote: Classify the support tickets into our six categories with a language model given instructions only. Show me the exact instructions, the model name and version, and where the text is sent.
findings.problem: The paste-ready brief has the assistant send client ticket text to a language model and report the destination afterwards. Unlike the 7-2 brief ('using an approved model') it sets no approval condition before any text is sent, against the course's own rule on client data (1-5, restated in 7-5).
findings.evidence: OUTLINE 1-5: 'do not paste client data into a tool that is not approved for it'; 7-5 seg7: 'Client data stays in tools approved for it ... ticket text sent to an outside model'.
findings.fix: "...with an approved language model given instructions only. Before sending any ticket text, tell me the model and where the text will go."

findings.quote: no method can score above their agreement
findings.problem: Stated as a hard ceiling, which it is not: a model can match one labeller's key, or an adjudicated key, more often than a second person does. What disagreement caps is how much a score above it can mean. The glossary of the same lesson has the careful wording ('cannot be meaningfully scored above it').
findings.evidence: Principle: agreement between labellers bounds how far a score can be trusted, not its arithmetic value; a model fitted to one labeller's key routinely exceeds a second labeller's agreement with that key. The same loose wording is in the OUTLINE brief and in tickets.honest_limits[0] ('caps what any method can score'), so it should be tightened at the source too.
findings.fix: "...two people often disagree about the main issue, and a score above their rate of agreement stops meaning anything."

findings.quote: against the rule the team already follows, replace anything older than a month ... next to the rule's twenty
findings.problem: Seg2 fixes the framing as one row = a creative three days after launch, target = fatigued within two weeks. No creative is a month old at day three, and a month-old creative's two-week window has already closed, so the named rule cannot produce 'the rule's twenty' on the rows the model is judged on. The capstone's worked example breaks its own rule that baseline and model are compared on the same rows at the same list size.
findings.evidence: Seg2: 'One creative, three days after launch ... Features come only from those three days.' Seg4 table: 'Fatigued in the top 20, model vs rule' on 'Creatives launched later'. Principle (2-3, 7-4): same rows, same list size.
findings.fix: Name a baseline that exists at day three, for example 'the twenty with the steepest CTR drop over their first three days'; or reframe the row as a live creative today with target 'fatigues in the next two weeks', so the age rule applies.

notes: Every figure in all nine lessons was checked against facts.json individually (narration, visuals, predict, quiz, review, drills, take-aways, glossary, other_ways, briefs). 7-2 and 7-4 matched in full. The two wrong-concept sentences (6-2 seg4, 7-1 seg4) are each the last sentence of a narration and contradict the rest of their lesson. Points about facts.json itself: (1) tickets.paired.method says 'same 300 tickets' and tickets.learning_curve.how says 'the 300 test tickets', but n_test is 450 and the paired counts only reconcile with 450, e.g. (147-39)/450 = 24.0 points. (2) tickets.what says 'a third are deliberately hard'; honest_limits implies 150 of 600 training plus 300 of 450 test = 43 percent. (3) Bag-of-words trained on all 600 tickets is 0.542 in tickets.learning_curve but 0.531 (239/450) in tickets.methods, while embeddings agree at 0.749; probably two featurisations (words vs words and phrases) but facts do not say so, and 7-2 shows 54.2 where 7-3 shows 53.1. (4) tickets.llm_misses does not say which of the two language models made each miss; quiz 7-3-q4 attributes the first to the stronger model, which cannot be confirmed. (5) forecast.interval low_pct/high_pct: the sign convention (actual relative to forecast, or the reverse) is not stated; 6-2 reads it as actual relative to forecast. (6) forecast.level_shift.months_until_back_within_1_point_of_normal is 4 for the regression, yet April is again 2.5 points above normal (0.044 vs 0.019); 6-2's visual note says so, but the single number would mislead a later author. (7) series_anomalies.naive_rule.incidents_caught = 6 includes the five-day slow leak (only the weekend spike is listed as missed). A 15-percent-versus-yesterday rule can only have 'caught' it through its routine Saturday alert on 24 January 2026, so that count flatters the rule, and the OUTLINE line that the leak is one 'the others missed' disagrees with facts for the naive rule (the lesson text avoids the claim). (8) Outside my lessons: tree.test.auc and tree.train_auc (0.761, 0.786) differ from depth_sweep at depth 3 (0.767, 0.787). (9) Answer-length cue: in 6-1 to 6-4 the keyed option is the longest in 35 of 40 quiz and review questions; in 7-1 to 7-5 in 9 of 50.
